prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which opened the 10^-18 regime of atomic timekeeping and precision measurement

statement.case_for: I opened with circuit QED first and optical lattice clocks third, and having read all eight ballots I now put the clocks first. The achievement is a clean invention-plus-realisation story: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removes the light shift that otherwise limits trapped-atom spectroscopy, and the lattice allows very many atoms to be interrogated in the Lamb-Dicke regime, which Ye's group then turned into record stability and systematic uncertainty near 1e-18. The result is independently reproduced at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, comparisons between clocks are routine, and the redefinition of the second is a concrete consequence rather than a hope. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: two laureates, with a conceptual originator and the leading experimental realiser. It also has the broadest opening support (six top-three placements, two first places, eight of eight members ranking it), which I treat as a signal worth testing rather than as merit in itself, and the testing above holds up.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that precision timekeeping with lasers and frequency combs has already been honoured (Hall and Hansch in 2005, Wineland and Haroche in 2012), so some colleagues may see lattice clocks as an incremental extension of a rewarded line rather than a new departure; Eriksson ranked it eighth and Danielsson seventh for roughly this reason. There is also a legitimate attribution question: ion-clock groups and the Sr and Yb lattice-clock groups in Paris, Braunschweig and Boulder contributed decisively to the performance records, and a two-name prize leaves them out. Finally, the case would be stronger if the second were already redefined, since that is the point at which the societal consequence becomes unarguable.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the clocks first as a clean idea with lasting impact, with Katori the originator of the magic-wavelength concept and Ye delivering the leading performance, and notes that combs were recognised in 2005 but lattice clocks have not been.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and with the timing argument, and it moved me from third to first. I would add one qualification to the 'clean' claim: Ye's contribution is not one experiment but a sustained programme of systematic-uncertainty reduction and many-body clock physics, so the citation should name the invention and realisation of the lattice clock rather than precision spectroscopy broadly, which would drift back toward the 2005 prize.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first and treats circuit QED as possibly too soon after the 2025 prize, placing the lattice clocks only eighth.
responses.response: On circuit QED I partly concede: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes an immediate second award in the same area harder to justify, and that is part of why I no longer place it first. On the clocks I disagree with ranking them eighth; the idea is original, the performance gain of orders of magnitude is measured, and a redefinition of the second is under discussion. On topological insulators I share the concern about allocation that Eriksson himself raises: leaving out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan, makes the three names harder to defend than the clock pair.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first as an instrument and detector landmark, and ranks circuit QED second and the clocks third while flagging that circuit QED might be seen as too close to the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I accept the instrument-builder argument for IceCube, and it is a real discovery. My hesitation is attribution and maturity: Pearce himself says the division of decisive roles among Halzen, Karle and Spiering cannot be verified, and the source picture is still partial, as Mehlig and Danielsson also note. The clocks give a more checkable division of credit and a mature confirmation, so I hold IceCube as a later candidate rather than this year's.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs experimental discovery first as a decades-long achievement that completes the electroweak sector, while acknowledging that credit is genuinely unresolved among Jenni, Della Negra, Gianotti and Virdee.
responses.response: I do not dispute the scientific importance, which is beyond doubt. My concern is that the prize rules force a three-person list onto two collaborations of thousands, and Danielsson's own ballot says credit is unresolved. I would not equate the importance of the discovery with the fairness of any specific name set, and I am not persuaded that a forced selection should come ahead of two cleanly attributable laureates; if the committee wishes to pursue the Higgs, it needs to settle first how credit is divided between ATLAS and CMS.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues treat lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes.
Whether the contributions of the Sr and Yb lattice-clock groups outside Katori and Ye, and of ion-clock groups, change a two-person allocation.
How much the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize should discount circuit QED, and whether that discount fades over a few years.
Whether the redefinition of the second, if it comes soon, would strengthen the case further.
statement.conflict_note: Potential recusal issue on B004: circuit QED is my own research field (circuit and waveguide QED, superconducting qubits), I direct WACQT, which builds on the cQED architecture, and Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson work in the area and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. The provided profile records no specific personal tie to Blais, Wallraff or Schoelkopf, but the committee should weigh my views on B004 with this institutional and subject-matter interest in mind. No specific conflict is apparent for B035, B008 or the other shortlisted candidates.
